about: Abila Station: early-1900s stop on the Pacific Electric Long Beach line; marketed as a real-estate opportunity, '20 minutes from center of town'; one of California's early Black settlements.
Africatown: founded by formerly enslaved Africans; now a historic neighborhood within Mobile, Alabama; a community carried across the ocean and rebuilt on American soil.

song: Africatown, Alabama Also seen once: Sandy Island, South Carolina

about: Allensworth — Colonel Allen Allensworth's 1908 Black city in the San Joaquin Valley; schoolhouse, stores, "we don't need permission to begin"; water cut, rail rerouted — sabotage by neglect; "a lesson in breath."
Antioch Colony: Reconstruction-era freedom colony in Hays County near Buda; formerly enslaved families bought land from Joseph F. Rowley and built a farming community of kin-based households.
Armstrong Colony: post-Civil War freedom colony founded by formerly enslaved Black families, especially the Armstrongs; a kin-based settlement community.

Bagley Park — a Black settlement erased by development: home deeds vanished from the county clerk's bin, runways paved over stories, jets overhead where lifelines were; "zoning laws struck like invisible hands." State unspecified.

Barrett Station — freedmen's settlement under the stars; Barrett's name a beacon; railroad tracks and cane fields; gospel-fire churches; highways splitting the community; "the soil remembers all our names."
Barrier Island: small African American island community rooted in subsistence farming and fishing (Gullah/Geechee waters); later faced land loss, displacement, and development pressure.

Beech Bottoms — 1870s freedmen settlement "under Carolina skies" (state unspecified — North or South Carolina); brick-by-brick building, church bells, then mob/Klan destruction by torch and rope; no plaque, no marker, no book page — "a scar on the map."

song: Land or Leave – A Tribute to Tunis G. Campbell
about: Belle Ville — Tunis G. Campbell's Reconstruction-era Black-governed settlement in McIntosh County (near Darien); ~1,000 acres bought and governed by Black folks; Campbell's stolen state senate seat; the "land or leave" ultimatum.
Blackdom: founded by Frank Boyer and Ella Louise McGruder; New Mexico's first Black town; an all-Black homesteader township on the high desert plains.
Bobtown: one of Louisiana's historic Black settlements, counted with Grambling and Mossville; Black settlement and self-determination in Louisiana.
Boley: founded 1903, among the most prominent of Oklahoma's 50+ all-Black towns; a thriving Black municipality in the age of Jim Crow.
Bookertee: small all-Black town in Muskogee County, Oklahoma; most likely named for educator Booker T. Washington.
Bowles: founded 1910 southwest of Fresno; a Black agricultural colony of some thirty African American families, organized through an investment company to claim landownership beyond Jim Crow's reach.
Bronzeville: historic Black neighborhood on Chicago's South Side, born of the Great Migration; home to Ida B. Wells and Gwendolyn Brooks; heart of the Black Metropolis.
Brooksville: one of Oklahoma's thirteen surviving all-Black towns, four miles southwest of Tecumseh; first called Sewell, renamed 1912 for cotton buyer A. R. Brooks; thrived on the Santa Fe railroad.
Brookville — free Black farming community in the Oakley area; Quaker neighbors, Black-owned land; grandmama's quilts, granddaddy's plow; the cabin still standing.
Buxton: founded around 1900 by the Consolidation Coal Company in Monroe County; a coal town with integrated schools and rare equal conditions, called a 'Black utopia'; faded as the mines closed.

song: Branches in the Dust: Cedar Branch Scripture
about: Cedar Branch — 1862 East Texas freedmen settlement in the piney woods; Levi Leonard's church and the 1888 schoolhouse; "never slaves in our minds."

Centerville — post-Civil War Black community on Maryland's Eastern Shore (Queen Anne's County); Liberty Street brick history bought with "Black gold"; AME roots; Kennard's halls and the schoolhouse door.

Clarksville — 1871 freedmen's town just west of Austin founded by Charles Clark (not the history-books Clarksville); Sweet Home Church still ringing; Mopac land takings; condos rising where seeds were sown.
Collier Heights: historic Black neighborhood in northwest Atlanta, planned as a Black middle-class suburb after World War II; listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
Cologne — Black settlement on Perdido Creek's bend, just west of Goliad; ~700 acres; a rare integrated depot; Jim Crow's dividing line met with entwined roots.
Cozy Corner: early-1900s freedom colony in rural Fayette County, founded by formerly enslaved people and families.

Davis Bend — Benjamin Montgomery's post-Emancipation Black utopia on the Mississippi River; Black-owned banks, stores, schools; "from bondage to ballots"; Klan terror met with defiance; a Black republic.
Dearfield — Oliver Toussaint Jackson's 1910 Black homesteading colony on Colorado's open plains; drought, Klan pressure, and the Great Depression emptied it; legacy of Black self-determination.
Deep Ellum: Dallas's 'Black downtown,' east of downtown along Elm Street; began in the 1870s as a freedmen's settlement and became a legendary blues and jazz hub.

Della — postbellum freed-people settlement on Maryland's Chesapeake edge; brick-by-brick, hymn-by-hymn town-building; church-centered farming community that Jim Crow couldn't bury; elders' oral history.
DeWitty: in Cherry County's Sandhills; Nebraska's largest and longest-lasting Black homesteader settlement.
Eatonville: incorporated 1887, one of the first self-governing all-Black towns in America; the hometown Zora Neale Hurston carried into literature.
Five Points: lower Manhattan, raised over the drained Collect Pond; one of New York City's first free Black settlements.
Fodice, Texas — East Texas red dirt, sharecroppers turned Black-owned acres, schools dug and built by hand, Houston County hymns, churches as gathering places; a town unmarked on most maps.
Fort Mose: established 1738; the first legally sanctioned free Black settlement in what is now the United States, founded by self-emancipated Africans under Spanish Florida.
Fountain Mills: small rural Black community in southeastern Frederick County, near Monrovia; a Methodist community of farm families bound tight.

Freedman's Village: a planned community for formerly enslaved people built in Arlington during and after the Civil War; churches and schools rose, until the village was dissolved and residents displaced by 1900.

Freedmen's Town: Houston's Fourth Ward, founded 1865 to 66 after Juneteenth; a thousand freed people filled the Buffalo Bayou swampland bucket by bucket and laid brick streets by hand; 400 Black-owned businesses at its height; a National Register Historic District.

Freetown-Port Rico — free people of color on "the island" (149 counted in the 1850 census); True Friends Society, Good Hope Hall; jazz and mutual aid; Creole tongues; a museum rising where artisans teach despite gentrification.
Land bought by freedmen led by Richmond; the Colored Industrial School; Adams in 1901; Booker sending the spark; Eddie's warriors and the Tiger band; "ink and steel, not bullets, got spilled."

song: Six Thousand Acres and a Seed of Fire
about: Grant's Colony: near Huntsville in Walker County; founded 1866 when landowner George Washington Grant dedicated 6,000 acres to a Black freedom colony.

Hall's Bluff on the Trinity River in East Texas — Joshua Hall's 1852 ferry stop, steamboat days, Black church and classrooms before the railroad bypassed the town in 1872; cemeteries holding names carved in stone.

song: Sanctified Soil: The Hill We Rose
about: Hope Hill, Frederick County — Black hands buy the church and ground in 1869; Hope Hill Colored School teaches before Lincoln High; Black landowners (Catherine, Irving, the Holland family) hold ground through redlines.

Hunter Street in Atlanta's West End before it became MLK Jr. Drive — Paschal's, Busy Bee, Abernathy, West Hunter Baptist, Ashby Theatre, Black-owned banks/theaters/barbers, SCLC blueprints, voter-roll organizing.

song: First to Rise: Heights of Our Own
about: Independence Heights, Texas — 1915 vote and oath, Black-led municipality, Mayor Burgess, self-made streets, grocers/barbers/churches, Ella Lewis's store; later annexed by Houston; roots unbroken.

song: Land of the Freedmen: Echoes from James City
about: Freedmen flee to Union lines in 1863, found the town on the Trent River under Rev. Horace James — 3,000 people, Black schools/churches/stores, self-rule; 1892 courts return the land to white owners; community endures.

Richard and Erasmus buy nine acres in 1874 from the old Aix la Chapelle plantation; build the two-story Jones-Hall-Sims "Freedom House"; farm and teach through Reconstruction; the Smithsonian later takes the house whole.
Black farmers on Huyett's land at South Mountain in the 1870s; AME chapel as the unmarked throne; tilled/prayed/endured without headlines; coded in trees, wind, unmarked cemetery.

song: Beneath the Water, Above the Chains: The Kowaliga Scrolls
about: John Benson buys 160 acres from his former enslaver; son William builds the Kowaliga School and the Dixie Line railroad; Martin Dam floods the town — submerged but unforgotten.

song: Ashes to Orchids: The Lincolnville Light
about: Freed people build the town in 1866 ("Little Africa," Victorian porches, Black high school by 1901); 1960s civil rights fight — MLK, Andrew Young, Hayling, Monson Motel wade-ins; Civil Rights Act born from a Lincolnville call.

song: Creek Code Chronicles: The Marshalltown Cipher
about: African-Creek Black Lighthorse police of the 1870s Creek Nation, between the Arkansas and Verdigris rivers; 1876–79 violence; pre-statehood Black legal code now ghost fields.

song: Streets of Freedom, Bricks of Will
about: General Mitchel's 1862 freedmen town on Hilton Head — quarter-acre lots, first Black mayor, churches/businesses/schools, Gullah Geechee roots; first self-governed Black town before Emancipation.

song: Ashes in the Bayou: The Mossville Testament
about: Jim Moss founding the town in 1793 with twelve Black families on squatter's-rights land; farming and postbellum industry; Sasol chemical pollution and buyouts displacing residents.
Black coal miners leaving Kentucky/Virginia in 1879 for Mahaska County, Iowa; building the town — schools, doctors, shops, self-rule ("The Colony"); homes moved to Buxton when the coal played out.

Newtown from 1914 platting by displaced Angola/Overtown residents; Emma E. Booker, first schools/churches; 1951 wade-ins at segregated beaches; National Register status (731 structures, 15 trail markers); present-day revitalization.

Quakertown, Denton, Texas, was a thriving Black community formed in the late 1870s around the Fred Douglass School, with homes, churches, businesses, and civic organizations. In 1922, Denton displaced its residents to create a city park, forcing families to move to Solomon Hill or leave the city.

St. Paul's Bottoms by Twelve-Mile Bayou — freedmen's creed, St. Paul's rising from flood-swollen rims, later renamed Ledbetter Heights; Jelly Roll played where elders prayed; jazz/blues where sorrow once laid.

Yarrowsburg, Maryland, in Washington County's Pleasant Valley, was named for Aquila and Polly Yarrow, free African Americans who bought land there in 1825. Polly, a respected midwife and daughter-in-law of formerly enslaved Muslim entrepreneur Yarrow Mamout, became the community's enduring namesake.
